title: Fractional GPU degradation recon, temporary fencing and rollout plan
content:
Summary:
We observed intermittent, per-GPU performance drops in a subset of the Dedicated GPU pool (region-us-west-2, pool-id: dedicated-pool-14) that manifest as 20–40% token throughput reduction for specific tenant workloads while other GPUs in the same host appear normal. This doc captures: brief recon of signals, short-term mitigation (fencing noisy GPUs at the scheduler level), on-call triage steps, and a phased rollout plan for a longer-term isolation + autoscaler config change.

Context and why this is different from typical noisy-neighbor incidents:
- Not full-host saturation or eviction cascade. Noise appears localized to one or two GPUs on a host (fractional).
- Affected GPUs show normal memory usage and KV cache patterns, but sustained lower kernel utilization (observed via nvidia-smi dmon and perf counters).
- Symptoms: elevated per-GPU latency p50->p95 (tokens/s drop), gradual onset over ~5–20 minutes, then occasional recovery.
- Hypotheses: thermal throttling in specific PCIe lanes, microcode driver regression for certain CUDA kernel paths, or OS-level interrupts/SMI causing CPU-GPU desync.

Immediate on-call triage (fast-path) — keep this on hand in pager shifts:
1) Confirm scope and customer impact
   - Query alert: promql -> sum by (gpu_id, host) (rate(inference_tokens_generated[5m])) to spot dropouts.
   - Check per-tenant error/latency dashboards (route:model, tenant) to see who is affected.
2) Spot-check host telemetry (only if safe):
   - kubectl get pods -n dedicated -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=HOSTNAME
   - ssh to host: sudo /opt/redwood/bin/gpu-health.sh gpuX (internal helper collects nvidia-smi, dmesg tail, dmon samples).
   - nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 5 -o TD (quick 30s sample) and look for utilization mismatch against expected.
3) Soft-fence the GPU in the scheduler (non-destructive):
   - Patch node annotation letting scheduler avoid gpuX: kubectl annotate node HOSTNAME redwood.io/gpu-fence=gpuX --overwrite
   - Trigger pod reschedule off that GPU by updating the node-restriction label (internal allocator will mark the GPU as fenced).
   - Expected result: impacted workloads migrate to other GPUs in the pool; short-term consumer impact limited by capacity headroom.
4) If fencing is insufficient and customer-facing latency is critical, perform emergency drain of host and schedule a rolling reboot (escalation to infra oncall).

Instrumentation and detection improvements (quick wins):
- New metric: fractional_gpu_utilization = per_gpu_compute_cycles / per_gpu_nominal_cycles (derive from nvml counters). Add alert if < 0.7 for 10m and token throughput drops > 20%
- Add a Grafana panel showing per-GPU perf counters (SM utilization, memory bandwidth) alongside tokens/sec for quick correlation.
- Tag historical incidents to detect pattern by GPU firmware version, kernel driver, and host SKU.

Recon notes from last event (2025-10-26 13:40 UTC):
- Affected GPUs: host-227.gw -> gpu1 and host-231 -> gpu2 (same server model: p5x-large).
- Observed: SM util stuck ~30–40% while other GPUs on host ~90%; memory throughput normal.
- dmesg had repeated WDT warnings at ~13:35 then cleared; BIOS firmware on host-227 was older than fleet median.
- Immediate action performed: soft-fence on gpu1, migrated pods, latency recovered within 8 minutes for most tenants.
- Follow-up: host rebooted and firmware updated; no recurrence in 48h but metrics show low-level flaps on an adjacent host.

Temporary mitigation design (fast but safe):
- Implement "fractional-fence" annotation and scheduler selector to avoid specific gpu indices without taking entire node out of rotation. This is lower blast radius than draining host.
- Fencing workflow (manual):
   1) annotate node: kubectl annotate node HOST redwood.io/fence-gpus=gpu1
   2) API call: allocator.redwood/schedule-evict?node=HOST&gpu=gpu1 (internal admin endpoint)
   3) watch reschedule: curl -s "https://alloc-api/redwood/pools/14/health" | jq .
- Add a cooldown label to prevent immediate re-scheduling back onto the fenced GPU until further inspection.

Longer-term plan (phased rollout — aim to reduce manual toil):
Phase 0 (pilot, 2 weeks):
- Ship per-GPU fencing API and small UI in Console (dev -> canary pool only).
- Add perf-counter collection to long-term metrics (NVML ingestion).
- Create detection alert (frac_util < 0.7) routed to SRE with a low-severity tag.

Phase 1 (1 month):
- Autodetect and soft-fence: when detection rule fires, automatically annotate node and trigger reschedule if pool headroom >= 10%.
- Add runbook automation stub that posts to #sre-pager with a one-click rollback (unfence) and runbook link.
- Telemetry correlation: store GPU firmware, kernel, driver, and PCIe link speed as labels on metrics.

Phase 2 (2–3 months):
- Integrate kernel and firmware micro-updates into the infra patching pipeline for hosts that show repeated fractional flaps.
- Autoscaler policy tweaks: prefer spreading tenants across GPUs to reduce correlated degradation risk.
- Experiment: tolerate minor fractional degradation (10–15%) for best-effort tenants with fallback to higher-tier GPUs.

Runbook (detailed steps for on-call) — quick reference:
- Alert lands (frac_util_alert) -> SRE oncall
1) Check scope via PromQL: sum by(gpu_id, host) (token_rate[5m]) and nvml_sm_utilization{gpu_id=~".*"}[5m]
2) Confirm whether pattern is fractional versus whole-host: compare all GPUs on the host; if >1 GPU degraded -> treat as host-level incident.
3) Soft-fence single GPU: kubectl annotate node HOST redwood.io/fence-gpus=gpuX --overwrite
4) Trigger reschedule and monitor tokens/sec; if reschedule fails (pods stuck) -> escalate to allocator team (pager: @allocator-oncall) with logs: /var/log/allocator/*.log
5) If fencing does not fix within 15min and customer impacts persist -> drain host: kubectl cordon HOST; kubectl drain HOST --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
6) After successful remediation, collect: nvidia-smi -q, dmesg | tail -n 200, output of gpu-health.sh, attach to JIRA and mark incident with tags.

Observability queries to copy-paste:
- Token throughput by gpu: sum(rate(inference_tokens_generated[1m])) by (gpu_id)
- Fractional util: (nvml_sm_cycles_total{gpu_id}/nvml_sm_cycles_expected{gpu_model})
- Host WDT warnings: rate(node_dmesg_warns_total{message=~".*WDT.*"}[5m])

Open questions and risks:
- Do we have NVML counters on all host types? short-term pilot will expose gaps.
- Risk of automatic fencing oscillation if false positives (need cooldown + hysteresis).
- Capacity headroom assumption: some pools run <10% spare — automatic fencing can worsen customer latency if not gatekept by pool-level policy.

Decision log (so far):
- 2025-10-27: agreed to build soft-fence prototype (Maya, Arjun, Lena)
- 2025-10-29: implement an alert and started collecting NVML SM counters in the canary pool (Kai)
- 2025-11-03: add cooldown label implementation to avoid flip-flop (Ravi)

Next actions (owners and ETA):
- (Arjun) PR for scheduler patch that respects redwood.io/fence-gpus annotation — ETA 2025-11-12
- (Kai) Finish NVML ingestion in canary pool + Grafana panels — ETA 2025-11-07
- (Lena) Draft automated-fence policy (thresholds, headroom gating, hysteresis) — ETA 2025-11-10
- (Maya) Run tabletop with oncall and allocator teams, capture runbook gaps — ETA 2025-11-06

Appendix: quick helper commands and internal utilities
- /opt/redwood/bin/gpu-health.sh <gpu-id> -> collects a 1-minute snapshot (nvidia-smi dmon, nvml counters, dmesg tail)
- allocator admin: POST https://alloc-api/internal/v1/node/fence {node: HOST, gpus: [gpu1]} (requires admin token)
- Logs location: /var/log/host-agent/gpu-health-YYYYMMDD.log

Notes to self:
- Keep the initial fencing conservative (only auto-fence when headroom >= 10%).
- Watch for firmware skew correlation — if pattern emerges, coordinate with HW partners for fleet-wide updates.
- This approach should reduce the blast radius compared to host drain and give a clear path from detection -> automated remediation -> human review.

END OF DOC
